summary: Friedrich Max Müller worked in Indology, religious studies, and linguistics. He earned his Dr. phil. at Leipzig under Brockhaus and others, and also studied under Burnouf, Bopp, and Schelling. He was a long-time professor at Oxford (1854, 1868–1900).

Friedrich Müller worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Vienna under Boller, Göttingen, and Tübingen. He worked at the Austrian National Library and held posts at the University of Vienna, becoming professor in 1869.

Friedrich Nietzsche worked in philosophy and linguistics. He studied at the University of Bonn and the University of Leipzig under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, earning a doctorate. He served on the faculty at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader was an Indologist and philosopher who studied at Berlin, Leipzig, Strasbourg, Kiel, and Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn and Ernst Leumann. He served as director of the Adyar Library (1905–1916) and professor at Kiel University (1921–1945).
Friedrich Ottomar Eduard Wilhelm held academic posts at the University of Munich (~1906–1919) and the University of Freiburg (~1919–1939).
Friedrich Ratzel studied at Heidelberg University around 1868. He later held posts at the Technical University of Munich (~1875–1886) and the University of Leipzig (~1886–1904).

Friedrich Rosen worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig, Munich, Göttingen, Paris, and under Franz Bopp and Henry Thomas Colebrooke. He taught Hindustani in Berlin and served as Professor of Sanskrit in London.

Friedrich Rückert worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He earned a Ph.D. at Jena, also studying at Würzburg, Heidelberg, and under Franz Bopp and Hammer-Purgstall. He served as professor at Erlangen-Nuremberg (1826–1841) and Berlin (1841–1849).

Friedrich Schlegel worked in Indology, philosophy, and linguistics. He studied at Göttingen and Leipzig, and with Alexander Hamilton and Antoine-Léonard Chézy. He held posts at the University of Jena (1800), University of Cologne (1804), and TU Dresden (1828).

Friedrich Schleiermacher worked in philosophy and religious studies. He studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1787–1790), where he later held a post (~1804–1807), before holding a chair at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1810–1834).

Friedrich Schrader worked in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg under Richard Pischel, earning a Ph.D., and served as a librarian at the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft from 1889 to 1891.

Friedrich Stamm worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned his Ph.D. at the University of Münster by 1919 and held positions at the University and State Library of Münster and the Göttingen State and University Library in 1921.

Friedrich Stolz was a linguist who studied under Bernhard Jülg at Innsbruck, Georg Curtius at Leipzig, and earned a PhD at Graz. He held posts at Innsbruck, becoming extraordinary professor in 1886 and ordinary professor of comparative linguistics (1890–1912).
Friedrich Streiter worked in Indology. He studied under Albrecht Weber at Humboldt University of Berlin from 1856 to 1861, earning a Ph.D.

Friedrich Weller worked in Indology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He earned his Dr. phil. and Habilitation at Leipzig, studying under Ernst Windisch and August Conrady. He was an assistant at the Harvard-Yenching Institute and held Leipzig's Indology chair (1938–1958).

Friedrich Wilhelm is a scholar of Indology and Tibetology. He studied under Paul Thieme and completed his promotion at the University of Munich, where he served as Privatdozent (1963) and Professor (1969–1998), alongside visiting professorships at Columbia and Collège de France.
Friedrich Wilhelm Graf is a scholar in religious studies and other fields. He held academic posts at the University of Augsburg (~1992–1999) and the University of Munich (~1999–2014).

Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling was a philosopher who studied at Tübingen and Leipzig. He was a professor at Jena (1798–1803), Würzburg (1803–1806), Erlangen-Nuremberg (1820–1827), Munich (1827–1841), and Berlin (1841–1845), and served as president of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences.

Friedrich Wilhelm Karl Müller worked in Central Asian studies, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Berlin and Leipzig under Sachau, Grube, and Gabelentz. He spent his career at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, directing its East Asian Department (1906–1928).

Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl was a scholar in linguistics and other fields who studied at Leipzig and Halle (Dr. phil.). He held professorships at the University of Breslau (1834), University of Bonn (1839), and University of Leipzig (~1865–1875).
